After having played this game for around 40 hours here's what I have to say.

Pros:
- Tutorial system is excellent. It provides detailed, structured explanations to bring you up to a decent level.

- Graphics are fantastic although the anti-aliasing could be improved but is fine for the most part! 

- Game-play is phenomenal, the flow of combat is extremely satisfying and smooth way better then MK-X.

- Fatalities are insane, the best in the series hands down!

- Sound design is excellent, punches and kicks sound satisfying alongside all the other weapons. Music could be a bit better however you rarely even focus in on it in the heat of combat so it's not such a big deal.

- Challenge towers. After the terrible and frustrating state these towers were in at launch I am pleased to say they are now doable and are actually quite a bit of fun. The rewards are varied with each tower and so you can take on the challenge to unlock gear, intros, brutalities, stones and player icons for your characters. You can also team up with other people online to take on a "Boss" type battle similar to tag team in MK9.

Cons:

- Varied framerates. 30 FPS in the Main Menu, Fatalities, Fatal Blows and Kritical Strikes and Krypt whereas the rest of the game runs at 60 FPS. This can sometimes be a bit jarring however I, for the most part, don't even notice it and in my opinion it does not detract from the flow of the game.

- Krypt: An excellent premise however the randomisation of loot and extremely expensive chests (13,000 for anything half decent) makes it so that you rarely get anything you want, with most of the rewards being items for the forge and challenge tower consumables rather than costumes and gear. Another thing to point out is that some items in the Krypt require currencies to use, mainly Kenshi's headband that requires orbs (which are used for crafting in the Krypt and are rather scarce to begin with) and eats them up at a rate of roughly 2 per second which is absolutely absurd! You get a large sum of Koins to begin with however once they're gone, and they go quickly mind you as everything is so expensive!, You can gain a fair amount of Koins and Hearts in a short amount of time however YOU HAVE TO SPEND KOINS TO RESTOCK THE CHESTS IN THE KRYPT!!! as once you've opened them they don't refresh! Meaning you have to spend even more time grinding for Koins which you won't get rewards from!

- Kustomisation: An absolute tragedy of a system, apparently borrowed from Injustice 2 (although I have never played it so cannot confirm) this system makes it so that you have to level up the gear that you wear in order to slot in stones that modify your characters stats in some way, be it bonus damage with a certain move or resistance to certain types of damage. Doesn't sound too bad right? WRONG! You have to level up EACH PIECE OF GEAR, so if you equip a new helmet you're back to square ONE!!! Also guess where all the gear/stones and skins are unlocked? That's right! the Krypt, so you have to spend HOURS grinding for Koins in order to even have a CHANCE at getting a piece of gear you want. Also you have to have the correct stone for the correct slot in that gear making the chances of having a matching set of stones for your gear EVEN SMALLER!!!

- Story. A crippling issue of audio video de-sync has ruined all enjoyment of the story. 
I'd like to note that changing the in-game setting all to their lowest settings HAD NO EFFECT!!. Such as shame as what I did get to experience was brilliant! 

UPDATE: A workaround is to pause the game, wait 5 seconds and then resume however while this does work be ready to keep pausing every 10 seconds as the game will quickly de-sync itself again.

Note: I have not had any connections issues or random crashes that other people have experienced however that's not to say these issues do not occur.

As a final verdict, which i hope will change in the future, I would still NOT recommend that you purchase this game and it absolutely pains me to say that. But it's clear this game has MAJOR issues. Even after two patches which shouldn't have been needed in the first place (it's like they didn't even play-test their own game!)  issues are still present, the story de-sync being a hard hitter, the RNG Krypt system alongside the awful gear level up system and augments are still major gripes which is a shame as the amount of customisation is great, just don't expect to get the gear or skins you want anytime soon, unless of course they pop up in the store in which case you can purchase it with micro-transactions!

A final note about the political controversy in the game. It may be a rather cheap shot to include politics in gaming. However, I personally don't hold it against the game and does not affect my rating as I am looking purely at the game play and mechanics.

[b]New characters, again[/b]

I'm using the same structure here that I used for my MK 10 review. Again, we have some new characters introduced in this latest episode. Geras, Cetrion, Kollektor, just to name a few. All with their unique look and special moves. And, naturally, with an important place in the new story mode we are presented with. The majority of those debuting in MK 10 return and some do not (I missed Tremor but was glad for not having Ferra/Torr any longer).

While the battle against Shinnok was interesting in the predecessor we were already familiar with the fallen Elder God. MK 11 finally introduces a completely new antagonist, Kronika, who happens to be a Titan (a rank greater than that of an Elder God) and also the mother of Shinnok. She doesn't like the idea of Raiden becoming strong and sees him as someone tampering with the balance between good and evil. She manipulates time in her favour and as different timelines (or perhaps it's best to say past and present) are merging we get an explanation for the presence of Shao Kahn, Baraka and (finally) for the non-revenant versions of some klassik characters.

Cutscenes are great and some chapters ask us to select between two characters. This increases the replayability. The only downside here is the audio glitch a lot of users reported - in every couple of seconds we get a slight audio stutter that apparently hasn't been fixed. Not that big a problem, though. Oh, and I didn't mind the removal of the QTE sections.

[b]Instead of expansions head for Ultimate[/b]

I should have bought Aftermath as well as Kombat Pack 2. I'm stuck with the base 25-member roster coupled with the 6 guest stars introduced in Kombat Pack 1. The DLCs introduce characters that were not present in 10 but only in episode 9 (Shang Tsung, Sindel, Nightwolf, Sheeva etc.) and once again we get characters from different franchises. Joker is here as NetherRealm is also responsible for the Injustice series. A nice suprise was Spawn (Keith David does the voice acting just as he did in the HBO-produced animated series) and of course Terminator, Rambo and RoboCop are great additions.

[b]Fatal Blows, Krushing Blows, Mercy and Friendship[/b]

Brutalities return and there are many (at least 5-6?) for each character. We can also decide to give some health to our enemies while performing a Mercy during the countdown for fatalities. This is good for two reasons: in case of missed brutalities we now have another chance and this also increases our score. Go with the Mercy+Brutality kombo whenever you can. Or pick the Friendship as it nails you 50k just as one Brutality performance does.

No more X-Rays. Well, they exist but are referred to as Fatal Blows. Instead of the gauges we have it is the health bar that triggers them. Only one is available for a match (so one for 2 rounds) and should an enemy block it we have the opportunity to use them again a couple of secs later (so one is available until you land it successfully). No more crushed bones in the animation but instead there is a lot of blood in slow-mo - this is the new effect introduced here and blood now truly looks realistic.

Krushing Blows are well-timed specials or even kombos. One is available for all characters: the uppercut. Do it when an enemy is about to hit you and you get a nice jaw-crushing animation and a great damage output. So, the effect from the X-rays actually returns. Pro players hate this as newbies such as myself can easily trigger them. They also hate that our gauges automatically fill up so amplied versions of special attacks will be performed left and right. There is a reason for me using plurals: we have an offensive and defensive gauge to separate the actions we can do with them into two appropriate categories. The game puts more emphasis on strategy than ever before. This is very well explained in the tutorial mode.

[b]For extra longevity: customisation and Krypt in the third person[/b]

Remember the character variations? We now create our own. Or modify the already available two for each character. We can modify the names and the variation icon, too. Our characters have several intro and victory animations. And there are 3 gear items for everybody. For instance, for Kahn we can pick the look of our spear, hammer and helmet. For Cassie it's the glasses, her pistol and the drone accompanying her. And this is just the gear (around 30 for each type) as we also have roughly 70 skins for every character. It is slightly misleading as sometimes only the colour is different but we still have at least a dozen distinguishable looks here.

The majority can be found in the Krypt which is now played in the third-person. Chests require not only koins but soul fragments and hearts, too. The more you need the greater the reward is. You can also tamper with the timeline and close chests so that they can be reopened again. This game mode takes place on Shang Tsung's island and we can even run up to the bridge that acts as the Pit level from the game (yes, the duel in the background is visible). The goal is to reach the throne room and to fully explore it you have to perform at least 25 fatalities on each 25 character (base roster). Once all the heads are put on their respective spikes you can get your hands on the last pieces of treasure.

Towers also return. We actually see islands / platforms as this is better for visibility. A platform can contain several towers. So, instead of having one with 10 enemies we have, let's say 4 towers. The first two with 3 enemies, one with just a single (boss) fight and the last one again with 3 enemies. Why? Because each tower has its own rewards and while the best is to complete the entire platform for the objective rewards an individual tower can also be useful for practice as they can have their own, separate modifiers. 

Modifiers that we can also apply. They are called konsumable and the game encourages us to do this as it increases the score we get at the end. These can be defensive (immunity-based), offensive (projectiles or character assistance) or just plain ridiculous (poisoned pie thrown at the opponent). Some of the boss battles cannot be won without these. We also have static towers - platforms raised for each character (for intro and victory animation rewards their completion is a must), towers where we fight bosses together with other players and we can also summon special towers provided we have their respective keys from the Krypt.

[b]Konklusion[/b]

I could go on but I'm running out of space. The content in this game is simply krazy. There are no more faction war weeks but a season based online league event is available; just recently hidden Kronika treasures have been added to the Krypt. You can even change the voice for the announcer - I picked Johnny Cage who uses nicknames for everybody. Hope NetherRealm makes an Injustice 3 so that I can properly finish this game until MK 12 is released. This game is a krowning accomplishment, a koup de mâitre, a krème de la krème.

Mortal Kombat 11 had the blueprints to be one of my favorite MK games of all time. The gameplay is fantastic, the story is actually great despite some missteps, an indepth tutorial for each character, a krypt that has Shang Tsung Narrating each new area. It had so much potential.....

Alas, all of this is marred by the constant online nature of the game. All of the towers are locked behind online, your currency, your rewards, and even the krypt is locked behind the always online gate.

But wait, there's more...

There's three types of currency, four if you count time stones( I don't count those augment coins as they practically don't exist for me), and they are gold koins, souls, and hearts. + Diverse cast with different gameplay, strength, and weaknesses can lead to a lot of replayability.

+ Story mode cutscenes are beautiful while the story on itself is good and resolves some of its plots.

+ Mercy can make combat online more exciting. The game is easy to pick but hard to master, making it a good entry for newcomers in general.

[h1] Introduction [/h1]

Mortal Kombat 11 is the latest entry in the Mortal Kombat franchise. With a revamped system, good variation in characters and more content for the single-player experience is one of the most solid experiences of this year. Crushing blows and fatality look spectacular thanks to the care put into the details of animations and models of the character, highlighting the trademark of gory spectacle that Mortal Kombat is known for. It makes for a strong entry for newcomers and veterans alike.


[h1] Gameplay [/h1]

The combat keeps the traditional formula with the integration of the new elements for the latest entries. Variations are still in the game, and players can customize their own to their liking, tailoring their characters techniques to suit their gameplay better. It is easy to pick up and play since specials are easy to use but hard to master as combos and mechanics require effort and learning. It makes it an ideal title as there is not a barrier to obstruct newcomers. At the same time, it rewards veterans for putting their time into the game.

It also helps with keeping the game fresh as there are always more things to master and that possibility of getting better, improving in the game. Crushing blows and special moves can turn the tide of combat at any time, and they feel very gratifying to pull out. Fatalities are fast and gory, making for swift execution of the opponent.

Customization options are abundant, not only in special moves or variations but also in cosmetics. It gives players more control over their characters with in-depth customization. There are revenant skins along with normal ones as well as more of them. You can personalize the intros, weapons, masks, outfits, moves, taunts, brutalities, and more. Customization on itself is never wrong, and it is good to see that Mortal Kombat wants you to make this your own experience to the best of its ability.

The roster is robust and offers a lot of variety even when some characters didn't make the cut. Some fan favorites such as Baraka, Scorpion, Sub-zero, Raiden, and Sonya Blade are in the base game. In contrast, others such as Sindra, Nightwolf, and Shao Kahn are a feature as DLC. As to the variety, there is a lot of options. Baraka is slow but can deal a lot of damage efficiently. Kabal has easy access to powerful combos. Cassie Cage is a zoner that can control the distance towards her opponent. Sonya Blade has powerful mix-ups that can be hard to defend against, to name a few.

Modes such as the tower of time present an adequate challenge for players to surpass themselves, giving the game even more replayability and features. Klassic tower allows players to explore the characters' endings. AI battles can be a fun diversion to partake in as you change the settings of how you want your AI's to fighting style to be. The krypt has multiple unlockables, and tournament mode is also a mode if you are interested in that.




[h1] Strong points [/h1]

Mortal Kombat 11 is a solid game, and it is overall strong across most of its aspects. It has very few weaknesses as a game, and it is a quality title. Some of the DLC, such as the Terminator, are welcome additions as guest characters. At the same time, combat is shaping to be dynamic and fast. I think the strongest point here is that the gameplay is so good, it is a lot of fun and rewards the time you put into it.

Tutorials for newcomers so that they can better grasp the concept of the game, while the Tower of time and Ranked mode will put their skills to the test once they are ready for them. There is a lot to work toward, and one always wants to unlock more stuff and improve their abilities in the game. The cinematics is enjoyable to watch, both in story mode as well as in fatalities and crushing blows. All of this allows players to continue their Mortal Kombat 11 experience.

[h1] Story [/h1]

The story follows the events of Mortal Kombat X, with Shinnok defeat and Raiden obtaining his amulet. The amulet starts to influence Raiden's thoughts as he becomes more violent and tyrant-like. It leads him into invading Revenant Liu Kang and Kitana castle in a preemptive strike with some earth realm characters to avoid any threat.

They succeed in their mission, leaving the revenants in a vulnerable state and allowing Kronika, an elder god of time, to put a power move and recruit them into her service. With the help of the revenants and other allies, she will set into motion her plan. It is how the story of Mortal Kombat 11 begins.

The story, for the most part, is solid, and it deals with some of the plots of previous games. The focus is center on the collision of past and present, which gives some new interactions of characters. The cinematics is beautiful to the degree that it looks like a movie, and it is an excellent trip to enjoy while exploring the story of the game.

[h1] Some Notes [/h1]

The game runs flawlessly. I tested it on both a GTX 1060 and a GTX 1070, and on both systems, high settings delivered perfect 60 frames while looking fantastic. The only thing that struggles to reach 60 fps what the Krypt mode, but overall it hovered around 40-50 fps for the most part. No crashes to speak of, and the online experience was stable even with opponents who only had yellow bars. 30 Matches in and no lag whatsoever.

The game features some micro-transactions when it comes to cosmetics. While some of them can be earned with in-game currency, most of them are expensive enough that you will need to pay for them. That only refers to some cosmetics. Most of them can be obtained via playing the game whenever that be unlockable in the krypt, received for completing challenges or other tasks. I never felt the need to get one of the pay for those cosmetics in particular.


[h1] Conclusion [/h1]

Mortal Kombat 11 is one of the best entries in the franchise. It is easy to recommend, especially when it is on sale. Deep customization, variety of modes, challenges to test one's skills, ranked modes. It features a learning curve that is easy to get into but hard to master, and this elevates the game's replayability immensely. With its rich details and care put into animations, this game manages to be an excel in most aspects. If you are a fan of the series or like fighting games, get it. If you are interested in getting into it for the first time as a newcomer, do give it a thoughtful look. It is a quality title and an excellent game.

There's been a lot of confusion over the recent "80 gig" patch and it lead to some unfair, and downright useless review spamming. So I figured I'd let anyone who's actually interested in the game know what happened.

The initial game installation was just shy of 90 gigs before the recent patch was made. MK11 is a game that tends to verify itself after downloading and installing, instead of just allowing you to play. This makes the process a real slog as you wait for everything to pass file verification. 
The current installation is NOT 200 gigs, though I've seen that number tossed around. I can only assume people are getting this total by adding the original 90 [i](rounded up)[/i] to the new 90 [i](also rounded)[/i], which had to be on the hard drive at the same time due to the way steam downloads temporary files/archives prior to patching. To make that as clear as possible, [b]The game did not add another 80 gigs to the initial installation size[/b], it replaced it. Steam just needs room to download the patch before applying it, and then removes that data afterwards. 

That being said, [i][u]this is a bloated game[/u][/i]. Sitting at a whopping [b]116 gigs[/b], this single title I use primarily for Towers and not PVP consumes just shy of 120 gigs on my primary SSD.
There's no denying that this is a bad size, but it's absolutely not the 180-200 people are claiming it is. If size is in fact an issue, then by all means add that into your decision-making. But the reviews bombing the ratings recently are neither critical nor insightful in any way and it should be noted that the game runs just fine. 
Performance-wise I maintain a constant 60 at all times there isn't a 30fps cap, no stutter in gameplay or audio, no crashes, no bugs have been found.  While I understand there are some mods that let you run the crypt above the frame limit, I simply don't care enough personally to try them.

Ultimately, the game and all of its features work and the entire experience can still be enjoyed. So giving it a blind negative rating because someone has a smaller hard drive is simply disingenuous.

[i]Don’t expect Mortal Kombat 11 to be a tasteless 1v1 online fighting game. It’s much more than that.[/i]

[h1][b] 📝Story/Plot without spoilers:[/b][/h1]
Earthrealm is being attacked by Netherrealm, and only Raiden can fight against the time controlling villain. But will there be a cliché ending or a twist you weren’t prepared for? Yes, the story is in continuity. But even with no pre-knowledge of the plot, you can still understand and enjoy the story. Narration is on point; cinematics captures every crucial detail in the story.

[h1][b]🎮Gameplay:[/b][/h1]
[b]Wrong mindset-[/b]
The primary reason people don’t consider buying these games is the mindset; “It’s just a fighting game where you spam controls and 1v1 someone locally or online”. Well, that’s just the tip of the iceberg. Mortal Kombat 11 is much more tactical and in-depth than you think. There’s no previous double dash player movement that used to help the player aggressively attack the opponent. Removing this mechanic was a better choice, as this slows down the gameplay up to an extent that both the players can switch to aggressive or passive gameplay with fewer randomness.

[b]Playing order to follow-[/b]
Consider Mortal Kombat 11 as a periodic table. All the moves and their difficulty are already set. Spamming them randomly won’t help you beat a player who did his homework and memorized the combos. So instead of jumping straight into online 1v1, use the brilliantly structured tutorial. There’s a tutorial for everything, but right now, you only need to memorize the key bindings for basic attacks. But why bother with story mode? You may ask. Story mode is the pathway that explains why these characters are fighting and what their motives look like. I would rather choose a character who is visually appealing, but at the same time, holds a likeable personality/role in the story. Learn the controls (tutorial+fatality), finish the story, check towers and Krypt, customize your character and finally, engage in some bloodthirsty PvP battles.

[b]Mechanics and improvements-[/b]
All the controls and hitboxes with animation feel more refined than ever. In my playthrough there was not a single instance of half clipped overlapping attacks. The transition between moves feels very smooth along with their impact on the enemy character. The crucial aspects of Mortal Kombat are the deadly and creative attacks. Even though they have a tremendous influence from supernatural references, they're all designed in such a way that their existence might seem accurate. A guy throwing pointy chains and stabbing the opponent’s eyeballs? I mean, yea, it looks pretty “doable” to me. If there exists a fighter with lightning powers, I am sure it will concentrate all its energy and electrocute his enemy. It has a perfect blend of absurdity and realism. Do I have to mention the popular fatalities asserting the power to send some shivers up your spine? Yea, that’s what I thought.
 
[b]Possibility of grinding-[/b]
Yes, 1v1s are cool. But why should I invest 100+ hours just repeating the same stuff? Well, now you can endeavour the presence of collectibles and customizations. When I mention customizations and collectables, what comes to your mind? Appearance? Yes. And? Just that? As expected! Mortal Kombat went not only one step but few steps ahead. You can change appearance, character moves, all basic and fatality animations, their artwork, recipes, character endings and whatnot. Yes, you can finish towers and unlock character ending cinematics, or visit Krypt and open loot crates for artworks and other stuff. Now, these were just object collectibles. You also gain progress with your player rank that helps player matchmaking and even shows the predicted win percentage during the match.

[h1][b]📷Graphics:[/b][/h1]
What the hell! It looks so badass. Usually, in other games, environment is the only graphic intense element. But here, you are blessed with beautiful backgrounds, gaudy characters, and the camera zoomed highly detailed animations. The use of light is perfect, it makes all the stages dynamic. Blood, bones, muscles, lightings, fire, ice, everything looks great in the game. 

[h1][b]📝Main Pros and Cons:[/b][/h1]

[b]Pros-[/b]
[list]
    [*]S tier graphics.
    [*]Smooth gameplay.
    [*]A lot of customization options. 
    [*]Interesting story.
    [*]Actually useful tutorial.
    [*]Good number of characters and varied animations.
[/list]

[b]Cons-[/b]
[list]
    [*]Some characters have slightly better moves.
    [*]Krypt crates are too expensive to open.
    [*]Have to grind for even fatalities. 
    [*]Micro transactions.
[/list]

[h1][b]🏷️Tips to new players:[/b][/h1]
Memorize the controls as much as you can. Without knowing a variety of combos, you are just gonna be a punching bag in live matches. Remember, every character has different controls for fatality, and you have to grind it. You can quickly access the controls anytime during an offline match using the pause menu.

[h1][b]✉️Miscellaneous Information:[/b][/h1]
[b]Krypt-[/b]
The Krypt is full of treasures and chests to unlock everything from consumables to brutalities, gear and cosmetics, and even fatalities! However, most of the chests and treasures need to be unlocked using a variety of resources.

[b]Augments-[/b]
Augments in Mortal Kombat 11 are items that can be equipped on gear to modify or enhance a character’s abilities. Augments can be obtained by playing AI Battles, completing Towers of Time and looting random crates in The Krypt.

[h1][b]😇Honest Rating:[/b][/h1]
Honestly, I didn’t expect this much content from a limited genre game. But Mortal Kombat 11 seizes & impresses me in every aspect. It’s easy to understand but hard to master. I am happy to say, MK11 is not just a better graphic rip-off of MK10 in any sense. If you are patient enough, the sale price is quite promising. Give it a try if your childhood holds these precious fighting game memories.

The last Mortal Kombat game I played was MK4, back when I was a kid, and I really liked it. At some point I stopped being interested in fighting games, but I always had fond memories of the Mortal Kombat series. I liked the characters, the weird nonsensical lore, the over the top violence... I even liked the movies, though that was probably because as a kid I didn't realize how bad they were (I found the new one pretty disappointing, although the brutal action scenes were definitely cool).

So when I got MK11, I was expecting a serious nostalgia kick, and while I did get that to some extent, the game wasn't exactly what I was hoping for. It was still fun enough that I put quite a lot of hours into it, and a lot of it works really well, but some aspects felt off or out of place. It may just be my old brain going "back in my day..." or it may be actual issues that would bother most players. I guess you'll be the judge of that.

[h3]Things I liked[/h3]
+ The actual combat (or Kombat as the game keeps insisting on calling it) is genuinely really fun and satisfying, with a pretty high skill cap, lots of different combos, special attacks and defensive moves. Quick to pick up, but hard to master.
+ Catching up with characters I remember from my childhood and seeing where they are "today" was nice. Johnny Cage is a family man? Scorpion is good now? Liu Kang is a zombie? What the fuck did I miss? (The new characters are mostly also pretty cool).
+ "Towers of Time" gameplay mode uses the classic MK formula (a "tower" of fights where each win takes you higher until you fight the final boss at the end) but with fun twists - unique modifiers and challenges, consumables that change the fight, etc. Gives you quite a lot of fun single-player content.
+ Customization is pretty cool. You can not only modify the characters' appearance but also their moves, which means there are many different ways to play the same character.

[h3]Things I didn't like[/h3]
- Requires a constant internet connection, even for the single player content. Lose your connection for 2 seconds in the middle of a Tower Of Time, and all your progress is gone. Connection to the MK servers sometimes drops for no apparent reason even if my internet is working fine (I found this happens mostly on weekends) forcing a restart of the game before connection can be reestablished.
- Grindy as f*ck. All consumables and customization content come from lootboxes. There are 3 types of currency - Koins, Souls and Hearts - and you get them from winning fights, getting long combo-streaks, doing fatalities or brutalities, etc. This means, if you want to truly progress, a fight where you didn't end with a fatality or brutality is a waste because you don't get hearts - so you just get used to doing one every fight. So get ready to see the same fatality over and over and over again until you absolutely can't be bothered to look at it anymore. From a cool thing you can do to get a brutal cinematic at the end of a fight, they turned it into a chore.
- Still on the topic of lootboxes - You don't just open them through some interface in the menu. What you do is, you go into Krypt mode, which is basically a 3rd-person semi-open-world exploration mini-game where you explore Shang Tsung's Island, solve puzzles, avoid traps, and... you guessed it: open lootboxes, which are just locked treasure chests scattered around the map. I genuinely don't know why this mode exists. The puzzles are extremely basic, the exploration is boring, the movement mechanics are serviceable at best, there is no real challenge or penalty for dying, and... once you've explored the whole place, it just becomes a really slow way to open more lootboxes because you have to run around aimlessly looking for them. Why?? Why put so much effort into designing such a completely pointless game mode that just gets in the way???
- The story is just... dumb, really. I mean, it's Mortal Kombat, it's always been ridiculous Kung-Fu B-movie nonsense, but I feel like they went a little overboard here. Time travel, resurrections, zombies, just so much crap that is clearly only there to try and find a way for our favorite characters to still somehow be in the game after fighting each other to the death over and over again. The thing is... if it's so easy to bring people back to life or reset the timeline or whatever, then... why does any of this even matter?
- The new final boss, Kronika, is just a terrible fight. She's immune to almost everything, so using your regular tactics on her isn't gonna work. Playing [b]well[/b] isn't gonna work - combos, special moves, throws, etc - all of these are fairly useless. The only reliable way I found to beat her is to... jump and kick. Just keep doing this over and over again until she dies. This is what the big final boss fight has been reduced to. I even managed to get a flawless victory against her a couple of times by just jumping and kicking. On hard mode. What a joke
- Inevitably, it starts getting repetitive at some point. There are many characters I haven't actually tried yet, so I could try to mix things up that way, but... I think I've had enough.


I guess the bottom line is - while the core gameplay is very fun, many of the things around it aren't. I enjoyed my time with this game, but I think I'm gonna be taking another several-year break from the franchise now.

Despite its name, Mortal Kombat 11 is actually the 22nd entry into the brutal fighting franchise that has captured the heart, and spines, of fighting fans all over the world for the last 27 years. It's safe to say that NetherRealm lost the adoration of their long-term fan base once the series went into the 3D arena era, leaving behind its 2D fighting roots and expanding to cover a vast array of unwanted mechanics and additions. With that said, and along with the help of Warner Bros, NetherRealm was able to pull this seemingly dead franchise back together with Mortal Kombat 9 (2011), and subsequently Mortal Kombat X.

As sad as it is to say, all good things cannot last forever. There are many aspects of Mortal Kombat 11 that will drive away long-term fans once again; especially those who despise it when companies dumb down mechanics and add pointless grinding in for good measure. Starting off with some of the good elements, it can be said that the story is pretty decent; you'll get to see a lot of the main staple characters alongside their past and future selves, and the roster is fairly all-encompassing when it comes to blending fan favorites with MK9 and MKX kombatants, while also leaving room for a few newbies to be thrown into the mix. Going forward, I'm going to be referencing Scorpion a lot since he's a main for a lot of people, newcomers and old fans, and his moves are probably the most identifiable to anyone reading this.

Now for the bad, and unfortunately there is quite a lot of it. This review is a tell-all, so if you're not here for the long haul you might as well move on now. About 90% of Mortal Kombat 11 is frame-locked to 30 FPS. In fact, the only part that isn't capped at 30 is the actual fights, which are capped at 60. This begs the ever dominate question in most aspects of life... why? Why does the krypt, main menu, character customization, fatalities, and fatal blows have to be capped at 30 FPS? Sure, we could overlook the prerendered scenes of the story mode and others, but the aforementioned just does not make sense. This is the least of Mortal Kombat 11's worries since there have been a variety of changes made to the actual gameplay.

As such, nearly every character's classic moves have been augmented to render using them in a kombo completely impossible unless you "amplify" them, which takes up limited gauges; for example, Scorpion's regular spear move is now abruptly ended by an uncontrolled sword swing so pulling an opponent in to unleash a devastating kombo on them is no longer a thing. You can, however, amplify the move to do somewhat of a kombo, but the limit gauge ensures you can only do it twice in quick succession. Long gone are the fluid, player-created kombos from MK9 and MKX, and instead in their place are clunky, pre-rendered kombos that honestly just feel stale, look unappealing, and dumb down a franchise that once bragged about how its players were the ones who created kombos in the first place; since MK1 was never designed for that type of gameplay. It's horrible, and anyone used to the previous two entries is in for a massive wake up call when attempting to execute anything that was learned prior. Additionally, you're now forced to choose certain special moves per character variation instead of having access to all special moves, and many of the moves that were introduced in the previous two installments have completely vanished; for example, Scorpion's Hellfire moves.

Moving on, let's talk about the grinding. As most gamers are aware, anytime that the Krypt is in a Mortal Kombat game, you'll need to amass currency to unlock the chests and other goodies within it. It's the same this time around, except now instead of only Koins, you'll need Souls and Hearts. All of these things can be gained through regular gameplay, but the amounts that you acquire versus the amounts that you need to spend are insanely different; for instance, you might gain 5,000 Koins, 8 Hearts, and a few Souls by playing the second easiest tower on medium difficulty, but you'll spend anywhere from 1,000 - 250,000 Koins, 250 Hearts, and 100 - 10,000 Souls per chest. I might also mention that the Krypt is MASSIVE; it's in third-person which is cool, it's fun, full of puzzles, Easter Eggs, and surprises, but it's marred greatly by the amount of grinding that's necessary to get anywhere in it. Your rewards? Cosmetics, brutalities, fatalities, Kombat Kard backgrounds and icons, items for the new forge, and Konsumables.

The Krypt isn't the only thing you'll be grinding for. Each character now has their own tower that you can buy with, you guessed it, Koins. The first tower is 25,000, and each subsequent one increases by that amount. While the first tower for each character is easy and straight forward, the second one will see you doing 75 Fatalities and 75 Brutalities, and even deeper into the towers you'll have to do 100 Krushing Blows, spill a certain amount of blood, and achieve other feats just to unlock something you've already paid for. And the real kicker here? These tallies only count while the towers are active. So if you did 50 Fatalities with Scorpion before activating the second stage of his tower, none of those counted towards the goal.

So I've already written two paragraphs about grinding, but how about a third? You'll also be grinding experience points for your new gear pieces. Each piece of gear, three separate pieces per character (IE: Scorpion has his mask, sword, and spear), needs to be leveled up to unlock augmentation slots. Augmentations can increase a variety of things for the character, such as certain skills doing increased damage, or being able to damage blocking enemies at a higher rate. Thankfully, as this has recently been pointed out to me, these augmentations do not affect online play. But oh, and you found a piece of gear that you like the look of more? Now you have to level that piece, too.

I usually don't like to throw my own biased opinions into my reviews, but I can't help but do that with Mortal Kombat 11. I've been playing this franchise since I was 5 years old. For 25 years now, and through 22 total releases in the series, I've managed to maintain my love and devotion; for all of the blood, guts, gore, secrets, and especially the lore. As one of the most long-devoted fans of Mortal Kombat, I must say that this entry is a travesty that bleeds together the once thick line between the Injustice franchise, and the Mortal Kombat series. As fans of Mortal Kombat, this is not what we want. We do not want Injustice 3.0, we want our series that NetherRealm and Warner Brothers have worked so hard to resurrect with the amount of work and effort that they put into restoring the franchise after the major screw-ups that the 3D arena era games brought.

In closing, it should be said that Mortal Kombat 11 has a lot of potential, but it's too much like Injustice instead of itself. NetherRealm has completely gutted the kombo system, and instead instilled their own kombos instead of letting players create them as they have been doing for the last 27 years. There's way, way, way too much grinding for Krypt items, which will ultimately lead to people purchasing whatever microtransactions they're going to implement in the near future. The 30 FPS lock is both lazy and ridiculous. I'll go ahead and say it... the Fatalities aren't even that great in comparison to MKX; they're honestly just okay, and the same can be said for the Brutalities. The story mode is the most appealing part of this release, and at least it allows the franchise another chance in the future.

[h1]An Ambitious Fighting Game That Bites Off a Little More Than It Can Chew[/h1]

[i]MK11 is arguably the greatest game in the series when it comes down to pure mechanics and systems. It’s a frenetic and exhilarating fighting game with excellent combo potential, fun characters, solid net-code, an INSANE amount of content, a very well-produced cinematic story mode, and possibly the most photo realistic visuals ever seen from a fighting game. If you’re a hardcore Kombat fan, a fighting game enthusiast, or even just a casual scrub like myself, there’s plenty to love!

Notoriously though, this game is front loaded with a ton of content gated off by paywalls. Now, fighting games are no stranger to charging a ton for extra skins, characters, and balance patches. Let’s not kid ourselves and pretend MK11 is the first to do this. But this game can feel daunting with the amount of grinding you have to do to get cool stuff for your favorite characters. There’s stuff you can unlock by playing the story mode and finishing each character’s unique tutorial mode, fine. There’s individual character towers you can summon to unlock unique skins and cosmetics for a character… fine. Then there’s the hundreds of randomized chests to open in the game’s krypt, the competitive online Kombat league, the AI battle sets, the limited run time towers of time that show up once in a while, stuff you can pay for with multiple forms of in game currency or real world money, and… holy crap I still need to actually put in time to spar and get better at the game by fighting other players online!

Fighting games are already a huge investment to learn, something that the average person can be intimidated by. By adding a universe worth of stuff to unlock through dozens of context sensitive avenues, the game begins to arguably lose sight of what makes a fighting game a fun and competitive experience.

What sort of saves this, ironically, is the option to set the AI to play for you. You can toggle the game to play through most of the towers of time for you and unlock stuff at a rapid pace. There’s also augments you can put on your character’s gear (don’t worry, it only affects single player, no changes made in multiplayer), which can make your grind through the towers even faster. Noob Saibot is HANDS DOWN the best character to choose if you want the AI to take control for you. In the hands of the computer, Saibot does so many moves that the enemy AI just can’t seem to get around for some reason. The AI that fights for you is terrible at avoiding environmental hazards and obstacles though, so you’ll still have to take control and win yourself during those instances in the towers.

The story mode is decent, offering impressive cinematics and music to bolster its presentation. Each of its 12 chapters (17 if you have the aftermath expansion), has you playing a different character than the last for about roughly four battles, sometimes five, and sometimes you’ll have a choice between two fighters you want to play as for… more replay value, I guess? I honestly found the fights in the story mode to just be decent practice for mastering every character’s unique combos. Simply go to their move list, highlight which moves you want to have appear on the screen, spam those and beat the opponent. You can up the difficulty if you want, but harder AI in fighting games usually equates to cheap frame perfect gameplay, all of which isn’t actually going to train you well to fight other players online. Honestly, it’s not worth trying to play against harder opponents in the story mode. You get some koins and skins for finishing each chapter which is nice, and the story has a couple awesome callbacks. All in all, it’s worth playing through, but probably not something you’ll revisit.

As the most recent game in the series, most players will be active in this game as opposed to MKX or earlier titles. The community is mostly non-toxic, with players online willing to spar with you and help you learn the ropes. You can join steam communities to play against friends if you want. Thankfully the net-code is pretty good in this game so your losses online will feel more like your fault than the internet’s. Good luck and remember to enjoy the game!

So, all in all, with impressive voice acting and dialogue, a decent story mode, a ton of customization options to unlock, augments you can get to level up your fighter, gorgeous visuals, and a ton of replay value, MK11 is one hell of a package. Definitely wait for a bundle sale so you can get all the DLC so you can live out every 80s child’s dream by pitting Rambo, Terminator, and Robocop against each other. All in all, a very satisfying entry in this beloved franchise.[/i]

The game in one word: [b]FUN[/b]. This is a great fighting game. In it's core, it is a better experience than other Mortal Kombat games. The gameplay is tight, deeper, with some new estrategic elements. The visuals are superb, with great art direction and details. The sound design is great and the music is much better than the latest entries.

There are lots of modes and content. The story mode, for instance, is very entertaining. The Krypt contains lots of easter eggs and fan service. By playing each mode for the first time (from tutorials to online matches), you unlock new stuff. If you play the tutorial for a character, you get a new skin; if you play the Towers for the first time, you get a lot of currencies; each Tower can give you gears, skins and konsumables to even hard matches; if you check the daily challenges, you get more koins, so far and so forth.

Should you buy it at the current price? If you're a fan o the franchise, [u]YES[/u]! If you you're a fan of fighting games, [u]YES[/u]! Specially considering there won't be another major fighting game in the horizon. And, well, the thing about fighting games is that there is a diference in post launch online gameplay. It's premium price to play the game with lots of other players right in the beginning, so you can pratice more.

Is the game perfect? [u]NO[/u]! So how about all this negative reviews? Well, I would say to each his/her own. I'll cover the bad aspects of the game, but I believe there is an overreaction in general.

The biggest problem to me is the always online requirement. For single player content (like the Krypt), that shouldn't be necessary. You can play some stuff if you're offline, but not everything. I don't have server problems and I'm always online anyway, but this is bad game design. Maybe I myself don't have problem with that now, but it's clearly affecting some players and this has the potencial to cripple the game in the future.

There is a lot of content, yes, but the average player won't be able to see everything. The grind is real *¹. I'd say that part of the game was overdesigned. But if your goal is to play game first and unlock after, the grinding becomes managable. Each character has about 60 skins, that being 6 or 7 unique skins with different colors. Do you really need all the colors? The gears can give you a unique look, though (maskless Kitana... <3). I recommend to visit the Krypt after saving a lot of coins, so you can explore it without much trouble.

About microtransactions... Who is stupid enough to spend real money in this game? The store just gives you limited options in a limited time space and you can get the Time Crystals (ingame currency for MTX) by just playing the game. You can get more stuff by playing the game in just 1 hour. This is something the developers could remove entirely and the game would keep the same. My impression is that WB asked for it and Netherrealm Studios included, but in the corner. It just gave bad press.

The problem with the 30fps cap in Fatalities, Fatal Blows, menu isn't really a problem (I'm a guy who played 4 players split screen Goldeneye 007 for Nintendo 64, maybe at 10fps...). This is the same thing from Mortal Kombat X and it doesn't affect the fighting itself. I get you expect options in PC, but it is not a reason for a negative review. If you really have an issue with that, rejoice because the game is not in Epic Store and there is a mod to fix this while the developers don't patch it *².

There are some bugs here and there, but the game is just 3 weeks in the market. There have been patches every week. About the female characters' clothes and some endings... This is subjective, but I just roll the eyes when I read stuff like this *³.

The game might not be perfect, but it's a lot of fun to play. You can wait for a "XL" version or something, but this time I didn't want to play the waiting game. I'm a fan of the franchise (Ultimate Mortal Kombat 3 being my favorite MK for a long time) and this was the first game I ever preordered. And it was worth it. :-)

[b]In conclusion, the TLDR version: this is a must buy game, full price.[/b]

While I did play MK9 (2011), I skipped MKX and didn't really enjoy my time with it after picking it up for free about a year ago. Where MK9 was the right amount of cheesy serious storytelling, MKX went for a more visceral and gruesome approach. I feel kind of weird saying it, but Mortal Kombat belongs in the realm of self-aware violence and just the right amount of crazy, but not gruesome.

So, Mortal Kombat 11. It strikes that chord between visceral and self-aware almost perfectly. If anything, MK11 is at its best when you can tell they had fun writing the interactions between characters. It feels almost like a museum, referencing the entire history of Mortal Kombat from the original arcade game to MKX; it's immensely charming. The interactions between characters is important, although they don't separate Revenant dialogue with Human dialogue in PvP matches on occasion, which can be off-putting.

The actual cosmetics you can obtain from characters is insane, ranging from recreations of classic gear to brand-new styles that fit the character perfectly. Except for characters like Cassie Cage and Kollector, which suffer from skins and gear that really don't work for them, and you can easily tell. Cassie Cage has these Mass Effect-esque skins that really don't work, and any of the skins that would work are given to Sonya Blade, oddly enough.

Now if you want to get cosmetics for your character, all you have to do is check the customization screen to find out where to get it. Once it was insane to grind out gear in Towers of Time, but after a recent patch, getting gear is as easy as selecting a character and completing Towers with the "Selected Character" reward. Character Towers also once had insane requirements like "75 Brutalities," which have been reduced to more manageable "25 Brutalities," and so on. The random modifiers that once plagued the game with insane nonsense, basically making the game unacceptable without setting an AI fighter to do all the work, have entirely been adjusted and made substantially easier.

The Krypt has also been optimized a little more, with Krypt events cycling almost every week with some of the most highly-demanded gear in the game to be obtained easily, even granting the paid currency "Time Krystals" in bulk. Skeleton Keys to open more of the Krypt are now very easy to find, and the Koin, Soul Fragments, and Hearts currencies are paid out in extremes, meaning you could easily open the entirety of the Krypt in a matter of days, compared to weeks. Although some of the skins and gear are still locked behind the slot machine known as the Naknadan Krypt Shrine, and the Forge which requires you to get rare drops of single-use items to make other gear, which despite my playtime, I still haven't found every item. (Also, some of the recipes are actually wrong, but luckily they've all been documented properly on other websites.)

I'm not much of an online player, either, so knowing that certain skins and gear are locked behind the Kombat League, a competitive league that has suffered from a myriad of exploits like the Forfeit Set exploit, or lagswitching, makes it undesirable to get anything, despite the skins being some of the best in the game. However, there are plenty of ways to play online outside of that, including lobbies and even an online training mode. It also has Discord integration so you can find your friends and invite them more easily, although you'll be just fine using the Steam invites anyways.

In terms of the core roster, I actually adore all of the characters, even the new ones like Cetrion. They all have a unique style, and I found myself playing quite a lot of them. I have personal reasons as to why I don't like Sonya Blade's face model and voice actress, but Sonya as a character plays very well. A lot of characters have crazy combo potential in a corner, and with the addition of the third competitive variations with some minor adjustments to certain abilities, some characters are more fun than at launch.

The Time Krystals are a paid currency, but seeing as how the only things you can buy are cosmetics, or Easy Fatalities, and that they basically give you these Krystals all the time for free, it's basically more of a "finish the gear checklist currency." The store also has bundles of gear and intros for characters in daily rotation, the price of these bundles also reduces if you already have certain items in the list.

So I honestly don't regret my purchase. As patches come out (which still come out weeks after the console patches since the game's updates are done by Qloc, a third-party company, but they actually do things compared to the horror stories of MKX), the game gets easier to play. The grind for gear is about 10% of what it used to be. What could have taken years has honestly been reduced to maybe a few months for someone who only spends a few hours a week playing, and maybe two or three months for someone playing it non-stop.

It's come a long way since launch, and there are still adjustments being made every single patch. It's honestly my favorite game in the series. Notice that I didn't really touch on the story, because honestly it leaves a lot to be desired, and the "Character Tower" endings are much better. They also do a "Kombat Pack preview" Tower of Time every time a character in the Kombat Pack is released, regardless on if you own it. If the idea of it being all online throws you off, I'd recommend it on a sale, but for me it was well worth the price of admission.

[h3]Story:[/h3]
I was genuinely impressed by how much the characters and presentation have grown. There wasn’t a single character I actively disliked. Everyone felt memorable in their own way.

[h3]Features:[/h3]
[list]
[*][b]Towers of Time[/b] - Basically a deep-fried version of the classic towers, and weirdly enough, I enjoyed them a lot. They keep rotating, throw ridiculous modifiers at you, and reward you with plenty of gear, konsumables, and other stuff. They can be frustrating at times but it definitely keeps the single-player from feeling dry.

[*][b]Abilities[/b] - Each character has equipable special moves that let you shape your playstyle and build combos around them. For a majority of the roster, this adds variety and makes them feel more personal, however for the other part, certain abilities feel less optional and more necessary if you want them to be equally balanced.

[*][b]Cosmetics[/b] - Easily one of the best parts of the game. Without them, I honestly wouldn’t have had nearly as much reason to grind. The gear system, skins, intros, and outros give you a lot to chase, and I also appreciate that the female designs feel far less oversexualized than in older entries.

[*][b]Finishers[/b] - Every character gets the usual over-the-top love: Fatalities, Friendships, and multiple Brutalities to unlock and use. Mortal Kombat 11 is one of the best entries to the series in recent years. Several new gameplay mechanics have been added (Fatal Blows, Flawless Blocks, Breakaways, Dashes) and builds on previous mechanics to enhance the kombat. While the game feels slower overall than the previous MKX, it arguably improves on certain strategies and pacing. The storyline revolves around time and introduces a new villain named Cronica, who is bent on reshaping history in her own vision. Despite the fact that MK games generally have outlandish stories to begin with, MK11's is alluring enough for fans of the series. There are plenty of cinematic cutscenes between chapters to keep the excitement flowing. This is by far one the most visually beautiful fighters out there; animations are fluid, character models are jaw dropping, and backgrounds are varied, imaginative and highly detailed. Fatalities and brutalities are as savage and satisfying as ever, showcasing the series' patented brand of violence in an artistic way. The soundwork is solid across the board, from the voice acting to the crunching of bones. 

MK11 features an impressive roster of both iconic and new characters. Two Kombat Packs were later released as DLC which added several classic and guest characters such as the Joker, Rambo, Spawn, and T-800. With 37 characters to choose from, there's plenty of choice for all kombat styles. There's a deep fighter customization system, with many skins and gear to collect. Set on Shang Tsung's island, the dark and atmospheric Krypt serves as the setting to unlock and open various chests filled with different pieces of equipment, as well as fatalities, taunts, intros, etc. Fighters' movesets can also be modified to create unique variations. There are other single player modes available apart from the main story such as classic towers and towers of time. Strangely the tutorial was by far the most difficult part of the single player experience with insanely hard challenges. Multiplayer mode includes the robust Kombat League, where players can test their might against others in ranked matches, with rewards on the line. 

Mortal Kombat has come a long way since its inception and this latest instalment offers plenty of content and a great kombat experience, adding to its legendary status in the gaming world.

Critical Issues with MK Matches:

While the core gameplay of Mortal Kombat (MK) is solid and enjoyable, the overall experience is significantly hampered by technical and balancing issues. Approximately 90% of my match sessions are abruptly terminated due to desynchronization errors, making it nearly impossible to complete a game. This persists despite running the game on a fully updated system with Windows 11 and the latest drivers.

Furthermore, character balancing remains a major concern. Certain characters feel overwhelmingly "pay-to-win," as they can spam a single move and secure victory within a few hits. Health imbalance is another glaring issue, where your attacks deal significantly reduced damage compared to your opponent’s, and their hits often register first—even if you initiate the attack. This leads to frustrating situations where the opponent’s animations override yours, suggesting possible script manipulation or unfair mechanics designed to prolong playtime.

On top of this, Mortal Kombat’s constant desynchronization problems make the game incredibly frustrating. Matches frequently end mid-session, and while this might be tolerable at first, it becomes unbearable when it happens in 100% of matches on certain days. For a premium game on PC or console, this level of instability is unacceptable and detracts from the enjoyment.

In comparison, a free mobile game like Shadow Fight 4 Arena offers a far smoother and more reliable experience, with no such issues. Considering MK's technical flaws, it’s hard to recommend the game, especially when its most basic functionality—completing a match—is unreliable.

If these issues are widespread across the entire MK franchise, it raises serious questions about the developers’ commitment to quality. Rather than frustrating players with a broken experience, it may be time for the developers to reassess their approach—or even consider retiring the series until these problems are resolved.

[h1]A game for a very specific audience. [/h1]

I haven’t played a Mortal Kombat game since Armageddon, so this might be indicative of how in touch I’ve been with the fighting game scene. So take this as a review specifically aimed at the average casual player. 


Before I get to the meat of the game, let’s get the chaff out of the way: Graphically it’s a stunning game. All the visual fidelity and fluidity that you expect is here, keeping up with their previous titles. The Krypt received, in my opinion, an overreaction, but make no mistake, it’s still a huge grind. There is a lot of content here. The Krypt itself is very nice to run around in, some cool little Easter eggs and references throughout and the puzzle elements to finding the unlockables and keys are quite nice. Currency is potentially going to be a problem. While coins are simple enough to get and you can do a tower or two and get enough to open a couple of chests, the soul fragments and hearts are another story entirely. There are a lot of different chest types, they aren’t very well explained as to how you unlock them, and when you finally realise how, you also become aware that getting the means of unlocking them is going to be a slog. 

This is compounded by other areas of the game such as the Towers of Time, which also require 25,000 coins to unlock their character specific versions, and which will require specific consumables to do some of the harder versions. On its own this isn’t an awful idea, it’s a fun little mode with some nice changes of pace and quirks. Sticking it behind a tax, for which you need to do regular towers for, starts to turn it from feeling like a game to a job. Time, as ever, is a commodity and everyone’s trying to get yours. It’s no less the case here. 

[b]On to the meat.[/b]

Objectively, this is a good game. 

It’s very apparent right from the outset that there is a surprising amount of nuance and consideration worked into the mechanics of the combat. The move away from the dial-a-combo, removing the run button, slowing the pace down and forcing a more deliberate and calculated process is objectively a good thing. This a game that rewards taking the time to learn the mechanics, rewards knowing which meters to use when, how to get out of specific situations, how to juggle, how to avoid being juggled, how to modify specific moves in specific contexts to your advantage. The tutorials are exhaustive, which is a good thing. They also produce rewards, which is a nice touch to just acknowledging the time sink of going through them. 

While this game is objectively solid, the skill ceiling is high and the nuance is there, it’s very clearly aimed at a specific audience. It seems like the game is geared more towards picking one character and learning them inside out, and more or less just ignoring the rest of the roster. Personally, I like a bit of variety, and there is variety here, but just experiencing it can become a real battle. If you’re the kind of person that just wants to go through the towers and unlock some endings, it’s quite simple, the basic tower is only five characters and takes max a half hour. But there’s a good chance that it’s not a specifically enjoyable half hour, unless you’ve done prep work and done a half hour practice session with the character you’ve picked. I’ve always viewed the basic towers as the character practice, but that’s not the case here. 

The pacing of this game is fundamentally awkward. There is very little easy flow to be found. Mortal Kombat 11 has a very specific pace. It’s deliberate, but it’s not necessarily slow. Trying to rush down everything to get through content isn’t really going to work – just closing distance can feel stilted and frustrating. Just learning attack ranges becomes an integral part of the process, and it’s jarring and infuriating when an attack that instinctively feels like it should connect, with a slight nudge of the shoulders, whiffs because the rigid t-rex arms just stop an inch away from a stationary opponent’s face and you miss. Character attacks have a very specific range, and you have to be practically standing on the other person’s toes to be sure of hitting them. There are not many chances to organically feel out some combos and variations here. Blocking is a matter of timing now – it’s not the instantaneous damage cancel that it is in many other fighters and previous Mortal Kombat games. If you don’t anticipate an attack, you get hit. So you’re going to need to learn the wind ups and patterns of every other character, the directions they will attack from, and so on. It’s an extremely engineered product aimed at a very specific long-term audience. At times it feels very much like the Starcraft of fighting games. 

Again, this is all good. I will never criticise a game for deepening itself on a mechanical level. It’s starkly apparent that Mortal Kombat has matured from a button mashing kung-fu arcade game into a defined and considered product. It’s a good game and I can’t stress that enough. But it’s not easily accessible. You will get perhaps 8 hours out of the story mode, including cinematics, and that’s your easy mode where you can do whatever. The core of the game just has an inbuilt wall to it. The skill floor is actually surprisingly high and as a result of the tailoring and engineering that is all too apparent, it’s worth keeping in mind that Mortal Kombat 11 has surprisingly limited accessibility. It’s enjoyable, but that comes with a choke chain and the game has no hesitations about yanking on that choke chain. 

This is an objectively good game, but it may not be for you.

Mortal Kombat 11 is genuinely some of the most fun I've had playing a fighting game in many, many years. My history with Mortal Kombat goes all the way back to the early 2000s; I had played some of the earlier titles in the 90s, but I never had consistent access to any particular game in the series until Mortal Kombat Deadly Alliance. From that point on, I was firmly established as a Mortal Kombat fan and purchased every subsequent game up until 2011's Mortal Kombat, only skipping out on MK vs DCU. By the time of MKX's release I had fully moved on from Mortal Kombat, ignoring it completely in favour of Street Fighter IV and Killer Instinct 2013. It wasn't until MK11's release in 2019 that I had actually touched a Mortal Kombat title for the first time in nearly a decade. My initial experience with it would end up becoming shortlived, as I was simply too deep into SFV at the time to care about any other fighting game.

Fast forward to the present and my perspective on fighting games has completely changed. Back in 2019 I had firmly squared Mortal Kombat away in the back of my mind as a fighting game not meant to be taken seriously. Mortal Kombat was for casuals, and I was a serious fighting game player. Nowadays, my competitive spirit for fighting games has mostly taken a back seat in favour of just having pure, unadulterated fun, and playing Mortal Kombat 11 in 2025 fills me with a sense of elation as if I had rediscovered my own joie de vivre through a long lost friend or loved one. Long, flashy combos are cool and all, but they lose their impact when the individual on the receiving end feels like they're playing a punching bag simulator rather than engaging in meaningful interaction with their opponent. Mortal Kombat 11 satisfies my desire for a game with short, snappy combos and plenty of neutral interactions. It gives me a feeling of satisfaction from a fighting game in a way that I haven't felt in a very long time. With every new fighting game post-2020 trending towards relentless aggression and putting your opponent into a never-ending sequence of guessing games and knowledge checks, with [i]full resources[/i] right from the start of [i]every round[/i] to enact said shenanigans, often with negligible long-term consequences, Mortal Kombat 11's slower, more methodical and grounded combat is starkly refreshing. The game has its classic quirks to be sure; it can feel weighted, clunky, and perhaps even overly simplistic compared to its own predecessors, but everything in MK11 feels meticulously thought out in a way I haven't seen in a long time. There's a clever balance between offensive and defensive mechanics, split neatly down the middle, and a powerful but restrained comeback mechanic that's there when you need it but has reasonable restrictions in place so that it can't be abused. Mortal Kombat 11 does start you with full resources much the same as its more modern contemporaries, but its mechanics are divided in such a way that the balance of power never feels overtly skewed in any particular player's favour; resources don't overtly dominate the core gameplay and their separation between offensive and defensive skills means that you have to carefully consider their applications. MK11 always makes you feel like you have a shot, but never makes you feel like you can simply bulldoze your opponent. In an era of modern fighters where every round can feel like a volatile explosion, heavily lopsided in one player's direction through one, seemingly benign neutral interaction, I really, truly, appreciate Mortal Kombat 11's purity of intent; every interaction between players feels thought out and intentional. Playing Mortal Kombat 11 feels like a deliberate engagement between you and your opponent's characters and the way they interact within the game's systems, rather than an exercise in simply dumping a flowchart strategy or a series of rapid fire guessing game simulations onto your opponent from round start, never having to engage with them or their own strategy in a meaningful way.

My perspective is skewed by the fact that I've spent nearly 15 years away from Mortal Kombat. I didn't play MKX so I had no real expectations coming into MK11. I understand that for many individuals MK11's slower pace and neuteured combos weren't the droids they were looking for. As someone who greatly enjoyed SFV for many years and felt disheartened by the direction taken by SF6, I understand what it feels like to get a sequel to a game that makes you feel like you were a victim of Jedi mind tricks. That being said, Mortal Kombat 11 [i]is[/i] the droids [i]I'm[/i] looking for: a heavy focus on neutral and slower, more methodical and intentional play. Rediscovering Mortal Kombat 11 in 2025 has been an absolute joy and I highly recommend MK11 to anyone looking for a fighting game refresh; especially if your primary mode of play will be in local versus, private online lobbies with friends, or getting lost at sea in a deluge of single player content that for the most part actually feels relevant to playing a fighting game.

Is Mortal Kombat 11 Ultimate "worth it"? I asked myself that very same question for quite awhile. Let's just say there was a lot of controversy around this game be it because of the way certain characters were handled to more mechanical based issues such as the rpg-lite augment system. That is why I snagged it up for cheap during a midweek madness sale!

In my youth Mortal Kombat was a strange contrast to the fighting games I usually enjoyed. While I preferred the gameplay found in Super Street Fighter 2,Fatal Fury 2, Killer Instinct,World Heroes,and even the "jank" Street Fighter Alpha 2 port I got at the tail end of my snes's life span, Mortal Kombat drew me in for "other reasons". Aesthetically it combined martial arts movies with a dark fantasy aesthetic as well as copious amounts of violence,gore,and even the most cardinal sin of them all here in North America, actual "sex appeal"!  Mortal Kombat was the "bad boy" on the fighting game block whom didn't give a toss! The more moral activists railed against this series the more we wanted it. Nuff said.

The thing is MK had a lot going for it beyond the obvious Streisand effect. Aka, it was fun and competently made. I was never good at the fatalities and the fighting was "stop and go" to the point I had trouble chaining combos. Unlike other brawlers,your timing had to be more precise here and for me the command prompts didn't feel quite as responsive. Aka, if you were a pro at MK 1,MK 2,or MK 3 you were kind of a big deal! It was not as easy to master as its' competitors/contemporaries which only strengthened its' hardcore appeal for many fans.

People like me were more appreciative of the series for the surprisingly deep evolving lore and surprisingly complex characters. What at first was rooted in outlandish stereotypes and cheeky easter-eggs became its' own universe as intricate and intriguing as any setting from your favorite Dungeons And Dragons campaign,anime,manga,or favorite fictional book series.

We saw many gimmicks come and go. Switchable weapons and switchable fighting styles for each character. Fighting arenas with traps in them. Storylines better than the movie adaptations from the 90's. "Challenge towers". Tag-team matches. Friggin cart racing and battle chess! An actual in-game economy. "Adventurer modes" in which you explored fully three dimensional realms or dungeons to unlock yet more content. The list goes on and on. 

Put simply you get more of that stuff here minus the crazy mini games. There's a story mode. An "extended" story mode. Tower ladders. Daily challenges. There's even gear to unlock which can be socketed with augments that enhance each character in various ways. (Because this is current year in which the rpg genre has invaded every other gaming genre!)
If you are easily impressed by triple A spectacle and prefer fighters with a lot of reasons to keep coming back beyond the competitive fighting scene MK 11 Ultimate is rather immaculate!

"But" your mileage is going to vary a lot. Why? Mortal Kombat has become the ouroboros onto itself. For every improvement another feature OG fans liked was cut out. For every character well balanced and faithfully recreated other characters are broken and their new biographies are not nearly as layered,endearing,or as intriguing.

What is here is a good game but one that had to constantly change course because in its' own arrogance,its' own self righteousness, and its' own hubris it "almost" ran itself off a cliff on several occasions. This is what happens when certain people at the helm are more worried about how the public eye will perceive them rather than simply being faithful to the established subject matter as well as the audience whom has enjoyed it for many decades. Ya don't spit in the wind. Ya don't tug on Superman's cape. Most importantly you don't snarkily talk down to your biggest fan named Jim! (Because he has a youtube channel with hundreds of thousands of followers!)

Lastly? It is deceiving when you pick up an ultimate edition and instead of all the outfits and "other goodies" being accessible right away there are still ridiculous hoops to jump through to"officially" unlock everything in game. Maybe some people have the time and patience to grind away but I'm getting too old for the backwards unnecessary ways in which developers pad out,lengthen,and delay earning rewards. (Rewards which I paid for up front by the way.)

Pros

+Far more here than the typical tournament based fighting game

+Looks gorgeous!

+Plays smooth. (A bit of the stop and go shenanigans remain but MK 11 has made it much easier to string together combos.)

+Lots to do even after finishing both parts of story mode. (Including Aftermath)

+Still into the dark fantasy/martial arts/cyber punk setting.

+Shang Tsung steals the show! (And is still best villain)

+Mostly consistent 60 FPS during fights.

+Nostalgia

Neutral

-/+ To some the augment system will add desired depth. To others it will seem like tedious busy work.

-/+ Either you'll like the cameo characters or they will feel "out of place" as well as entirely unnecessary. (Spawn is a good fit for Mortal Kombat but every other guest character came off as so random or as a complete cash grab!)

Cons

-Even after paying for the premium addition a lot of the content is still locked behind  steep requirements and numerous challenge towers.

-Sindel's "reimagining".

-What Mileena fans had to put up with just to get her back in a dlc pack.

-Please keep "current earth realm politics" out of Edenia. Thanks!

- The game ran great for me "except" The Krpyt.

-Character balance is very hit and miss.

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
+ Decent, albiet tedious tutorial
+ Lobbies

[h1]Cons:[/h1]
- 30 FPS fatalities
- Horrible unlockables (in more ways than one)
- Pretty lame roster
- The tower modifiers

[h1]In-depth:[/h1]
There is a good game here. Somewhere. It is, however, very well hidden behind it's glaring issues.

Let's start with the one that affected my personal enjoyment the most. While the game itself runs perfectly at 60 FPS, the menus, the character intros and arguably the most important thing about Mortal Kombat, fatalities, run at 30. It looks very choppy, it's immediately obvious and it's just atrocious. This is the first Mortal Kombat game where I straight up don't want to use fatalities, because this ugliness ruins the whole match for me.

The other problem is the krypt. I don't even know where to start with this one.
I hated it in MK9. I hated it in MKX. But I never hated it as much as I do in this one.
Previously, you had to navigate this dull dungeon to unlock things. Things that were essential, like the aforementioned fatalities, because if you don't unlock it, you can't use it even if you know the input. It's already bad enough. But at least you could use the guides to find the chests you need in 9 and 10, so you unlock exactly what you want instead of random bullshit.
In this one? It's lootboxes. Straight up lootboxes with random chance of getting some crap. Seriously... why is this a thing?
But that's not it. They didn't just put random crap in it, stuff like boosters and modifier immunities (hold this thought, I'll be back with these later), but even the costumes that you can unlock aren't unique. Every character has 4 or 5 costumes. Each costume has 10 variations. And by variations I mean slightly different colors. So maybe you luck out and get a costume in your lootbox... maybe even for a character you wanted... oh... but wait... it's just a recolor. I don't even...
And by the way, did I mention that the krypt also runs at 30 FPS?

Ok. Now. About the arcade towers, as in, your main source of farming for krypt and most likely your main source of fun (aside from multiplayer). This time, arcade has modifiers in it. Say, random homing missiles that attack you. Or a place that drains your meters and gives it to opponents. Or just fire from the ground. It would be fine if it worked on both you and your opponent. But instead, they are only harmful to you. This is not the fun difficulty. This is incredibly frustrating. And it's made this way for one purpose only. To make you use the aforementioned modifier immunities. Which you can get randomly in krypt. Good luck getting the one you need.

At this point I'm not even gonna bother mentioning the failed launch of this game, crashes, roster that was cut to hell, extremely dull outfits etc.

This game has a fun story mode with good voice acting, a decent tutorial, acceptable fighting mechanics... and hey, it has custom lobbies at launch (learn from this, Dead or Alive :P ).
Fix the stupid 30 FPS fatalities, remove this dumb krypt and I can probably forgive everything else. But until then, this game will get no positive review from me.
